title: Unilateral cleft lip repair
subtitle: Anthropometric marking, orbicularis oris reconstruction and primary nasal repair

sources.title: Unilateral cleft lip repair: an anatomical subunit approximation technique
Parameters for Evaluation and Treatment of Patients with Cleft Lip/Palate or Other Craniofacial Differences

indications: Unilateral cleft lip, usually repaired at about three to six months of age as part of a multidisciplinary cleft team pathway.
contraindications: An infant not fit for anaesthesia (feeding, weight gain, respiratory infection, cardiac or syndromic issues not yet assessed).
Surgery outside a cleft team without the feeding, speech, dental and hearing follow-up.
preparation: Cleft team assessment: feeding, weight, syndrome screening and cardiac review where indicated; presurgical orthopaedics if used.
Haemoglobin and anaesthetic assessment; a recent upper respiratory infection delays surgery.
Consent with the parents: bleeding, infection, wound breakdown, scar and lip asymmetry, the likely need for further operations as the child grows, and feeding after surgery.
positioning: Supine with a shoulder roll and the head on a ring, the oral RAE tube taped in the midline of the lower lip; the whole face prepared, eyes protected.
equipment: Fine plastic surgery set, calipers, marking pen with methylene blue and a tattoo needle, 15 and 11 blades, fine skin hooks, bipolar, 5-0 and 6-0 absorbable sutures, 6-0 or 7-0 skin sutures, local anaesthetic with adrenaline dosed by weight.
anatomy: The lip landmarks: Cupid's bow peaks and its low point, the white roll and vermilion, the philtral columns, the alar base and the columella.
The orbicularis oris, which in a cleft inserts abnormally into the alar base and columella instead of crossing the lip; the lower lateral nasal cartilage, displaced on the cleft side.
criticalSafety: Mark the landmarks precisely before any infiltration distorts them, and tattoo key points.
Repair the orbicularis oris as a continuous muscle sling: it is the functional core of the repair.
Align the white roll exactly; a 1 mm step is visible for life.
commonErrors: A short lip on the cleft side.
complications: Short lip, whistle deformity, notching of the vermilion.
Airway obstruction or bleeding in the first hours.
postop: Arm restraints or splints per unit practice; feeding resumed early by the method the team advises.
Keep the wound clean; suture removal or absorbable sutures per technique.
Cleft team follow-up for speech, hearing, dental, palate repair timing and later revisions.

steps.emphasis: Consent with the parents; confirm the side of the cleft.
Weight, feeding, haemoglobin and no recent respiratory infection.
Supine, shoulder roll, head ring, RAE tube in the midline of the lower lip.
Agree tube position and the plan for blood in the airway; a throat pack is placed and recorded.
The whole face prepared so symmetry can be judged; eyes protected.
Local anaesthetic with adrenaline by weight, after the marks are tattooed.
Bipolar only; check the labial arteries before closing the mucosa.
Throat pack out and counted, blood cleared from the pharynx.
Hand over to recovery: airway, nose, feeding and arm restraint plan.

step.cl.markings.title: Anthropometric marking and tattooing
step.cl.markings.why: The repair is only as good as its marks. Local anaesthetic swells the lip, so key points are marked and tattooed first and measured with calipers.
how: Mark Cupid's bow peaks and low point on the non-cleft side, and the corresponding peak on the cleft side (Noordhoff's point) where the white roll and vermilion are fullest.
Mark the alar bases, the columella base and the planned incisions per the chosen technique (rotation-advancement or anatomical subunit).
Measure the heights on each side with calipers; tattoo the key points with methylene blue.
pitfalls: Choosing the cleft-side peak where the white roll is deficient.

step.cl.incisions.title: Incisions and release of the lateral lip
step.cl.incisions.why: The incisions create the flaps that lengthen the medial side and bring the lateral side across; the lateral lip must be released enough to close without tension.
how: Incise along the marks through skin with a fine blade.
Release the lateral lip element from the maxilla in the supraperiosteal plane so it advances without tension.
Free the abnormal muscle attachments from the alar base and columella.
pitfalls: Insufficient release giving a tight closure.

step.cl.nose.title: Primary nasal repair
step.cl.nose.why: The cleft-side alar cartilage is displaced; repositioning it at the first operation improves nasal symmetry as the child grows.
how: Dissect the alar cartilage off the overlying skin through the existing incisions.
Reposition the alar base and support the cartilage with sutures or a bolster per technique.

step.cl.muscle.title: Reconstructing the orbicularis oris
step.cl.muscle.why: The muscle is the functional core of the lip. Rejoining it as a continuous sling gives lip movement and prevents the scar widening and the lip notching.
how: Separate the orbicularis from the skin and mucosa on both sides for a few millimetres.
Bring the muscle ends together across the cleft, overlapping slightly, with interrupted absorbable sutures from the nasal floor down to the vermilion.
Recreate the alar base and the nasal sill above it.
pitfalls: Leaving the muscle attached to the alar base.

step.cl.closure.title: Mucosa, skin and vermilion closure
step.cl.closure.why: Exact alignment of the white roll and the vermilion-mucosa junction is what people see; a small step is visible for life.
how: Close the oral mucosa with absorbable sutures.
Place the key suture at the white roll first, aligning it exactly.
Close the skin with fine sutures and the vermilion with absorbable sutures, matching its fullness so there is no whistle deformity.
pitfalls: A short lip on the cleft side.
